info.name: Event Forge API
info.description:
HTTP surface of `@repo/server` (NestJS).

**Prefixes**
- Every API route is mounted under `api/v1` (`app.setGlobalPrefix`).
- `/health` is *excluded* from the prefix so infra probes keep a stable path across API versions.
- `/uploads/*` is also outside the prefix — a stored `heroImageUrl` must outlive the version that wrote it.

**Getting started**: `pnpm db:up && pnpm db:fresh`, then `pnpm dev`. Run the **Catalog · Venues** folder first — it fills the ids the create-event request needs.

**Auth**: none. Every endpoint is open; authorization is Slice 4.

**Errors**: all endpoints return the flat shape from `@repo/contracts/shared` — `{ statusCode, code, message, details?, path, timestamp }`, where `code` is one of `VALIDATION_FAILED`, `NOT_FOUND`, `CONFLICT`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, `ALLOCATION_UNAVAILABLE`, `EVENT_NOT_ON_SALE`, `INTERNAL`.

Optional UUID identifying the claimant. Left blank, the server mints an anonymous one.
From the seed (`pnpm db:seed`). There is no venues endpoint yet.

item.name: Health
item.description: Liveness probe. Outside the versioned prefix and outside the throttler (`@SkipThrottle`).

request.description:
`GET /health` → `200 { "message": "ok" }`.

Note the missing `api/v1`: this path is deliberately stable across API versions.

item.name: Catalog · Venues
item.description:
Read-only discovery. `VenuesController`, routed at `venues`.

Nothing here writes — venues and seat maps arrive with `pnpm db:seed`. These exist so `POST /events` is callable: it demands a `venueId`, a `seatMapId` and `sectionIds`, and this is where a client learns them.

**Run these two first.** Their test scripts fill `{{venueId}}`, `{{seatMapId}}` and `{{sectionId}}`, which 'Create event' then uses.

query.description: Free text over the venue name (1–120 chars). ILIKE, case-insensitive.

request.description:
`GET /api/v1/venues` → `200 { items: VenueSummary[], meta }`.

`VenueSummary` = `{ id, name, city, country }` — the same shape embedded in every event.

Ordered by city, then name, then id. The id tiebreak is not decoration: without a total order two venues sharing a name in a city can swap between queries and slip across a page boundary.

Unlike the event listing there is no visibility filter — a building has no status to hide behind.

The test script stores the first result in `{{venueId}}`.

exec: console.log('Sections to price:', map.sections.map((s) => s.name + ' (' + s.capacity + ')').join(', '));

request.description:
`GET /api/v1/venues/:venueId/seat-maps` → `200 { items: SeatMap[] }`.

By **venue id**, not a slug — a venue is a building, not a page anyone links to.

```
{ id, name, capacity, sections: [{ id, name, kind, capacity }] }
```

`capacity` is the **resolved unit count**, not the nullable column behind it: seats for a `seated` section, the counter for `general_admission`. The seat map's `capacity` is those summed — what Inventory snapshots at publish.

**No pagination.** A venue's layouts are bounded by the building, so there is no page to ask for; the envelope is kept so the response stays an object.

`404 NOT_FOUND` when the venue does not exist — deliberately not an empty list, so a mistyped id does not read as a seeding problem. A real venue with no layouts *does* return `[]`, and a layout with no sections comes back with `capacity: 0`, because that is exactly the state that makes a later publish fail with `empty_seat_map`.

The test script stores the first non-empty layout in `{{seatMapId}}` and its first section in `{{sectionId}}`, and logs every section — **price all of them** or publish refuses with `Unpriced: <name>`.

item.name: Catalog · Events
item.description: Reading and creating events. `EventsController`, routed at `events`.

query.description: date_asc | date_desc | price_asc | title_asc. Default date_asc.
Free text over title and venue name (1–120 chars).
music | sports | theatre | conference | comedy | festival. An unknown value is a 400, not an ignored filter.
ISO datetime. Inclusive lower bound on startsAt.
ISO datetime. Inclusive upper bound on startsAt.

request.description:
`GET /api/v1/events` → `200 { items: EventSummary[], meta: { page, pageSize, total, pageCount } }`.

Only `published` and `on_sale` events are visible here (`PUBLIC_EVENT_STATUSES`); a `draft` you just created will **not** appear.

The test script stores the first result in `{{eventId}}` / `{{eventSlug}}`.

`GET /api/v1/events/:slug` → `200 EventDetail`.

By **slug**, not id: reads address the public human-facing handle. Transitions (below) address the id instead, so publishing does not break when marketing rewrites the slug.

`EventDetail` = `EventSummary` + `description`, `doorsOpenAt`, `priceTiers[]`.

`POST /api/v1/events` → `201 EventDetail`.

Always produces a **draft** — the body has no `status` field on purpose; moving to `published`/`on_sale` is a transition with its own rules.

Body rules enforced by `createEventSchema`:
- `slug` lowercase-hyphenated, ≤180 chars
- `endsAt` ≥ `startsAt`; `doorsOpenAt` ≤ `startsAt`
- 1–20 `priceTiers`, unique names, **one shared currency**
- a section may be priced by at most one tier
- `seatMapId` must belong to `venueId` (checked server-side)

Getting the ids: run **Catalog · Venues → List venues**, then **List a venue's seat maps**. Those fill `{{venueId}}`, `{{seatMapId}}` and `{{sectionId}}` for you.

`{{organizerId}}` has no endpoint yet and still comes from the seed (`SELECT id FROM organizers LIMIT 1;`).

The body below prices **one** section. A layout usually has several, and publish refuses until every one is priced — the seat-maps response lists them all, so add a tier per section.

item.name: Catalog · Event lifecycle
item.description: State transitions and the hero image sub-resource. Each is a verb on its own route rather than a PATCH carrying a field — publishing settles capacity and hands it to Inventory, going on sale settles timing.

request.description:
`POST /api/v1/events/:id/publish` → `200 EventDetail` (draft → published).

**200, not 201** — it creates nothing; the event comes back so the caller can see the status it landed in.

Guards: a seat map, real capacity, every section priced. Per ADR-0006 this also makes Inventory snapshot the layout into allocations, so it is the step that has to happen before availability returns anything.

`POST /api/v1/events/:id/on-sale` → `200 EventDetail` (published → on_sale).

Only an `on_sale` event accepts holds — anything else refuses with `409 EVENT_NOT_ON_SALE`.

formdata.description: The field name is fixed by HERO_IMAGE_FIELD. JPEG or PNG, ≤ 5 MiB, exactly one file.

request.description:
`POST /api/v1/events/:id/hero-image` → `200 EventDetail`.

`multipart/form-data`, file in the **`file`** field. Pick a local file in the Body tab — Postman sets the boundary itself, so do not add a `Content-Type` header by hand.

Accepted: `image/jpeg`, `image/png` (`.jpg`/`.jpeg`/`.png`), max 5 MiB, `files: 1`.

Filename and Content-Type are client claims — the server also inspects the bytes, so a mislabelled file is a 400. Over the size cap you get `413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`.

Omitting the field entirely is a `400` malformed request, not a rejected image.

The returned `heroImageUrl` points at `/uploads/...` (see the last folder).

item.name: Inventory · Availability & holds
item.description:
`HoldsController`, routed at `events/:eventId` — a claim is meaningless without the event it is against, so these are nested rather than top-level `/holds`.

Requires the event to have been published (allocations exist) and, for holds, to be `on_sale`.

query.description: Boolean-ish string. Default false. Hides rows with nothing left.

request.description:
`GET /api/v1/events/:eventId/availability` → `200 { items: AllocationAvailability[], meta }`.

The path takes an **event id (UUID)**, not a slug.

Each item: `{ id, kind: 'seated' | 'general_admission', sectionName, rowLabel, seatLabel, capacity, available }`. `id` is Inventory's allocation id — the id a hold names, and the only way a client learns one until seat maps are rendered.

`available` is `capacity - held - reserved` **at the instant of the read** and is stale on arrival by design; a hold re-decides under a lock rather than trusting what a client was shown.

The test script stores the first sellable allocation in `{{allocationId}}`.

`POST /api/v1/events/:eventId/holds` → `201 Hold`.

Body: `{ holderId?: uuid, lines: [{ allocationId: uuid, quantity?: int 1–10 }] }`, 1–20 lines. Omit `holderId` and the server mints an anonymous one — identity is Slice 4. The event id comes from the **path only**; putting it in the body too would be two places to disagree.

A seat is always `quantity: 1` (its capacity makes anything else impossible); a general-admission counter takes N in one line.

Failure modes — the whole point of the endpoint is telling them apart:

| Status | code | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | Malformed body, or a repeated line |
| 404 | `NOT_FOUND` | No such event, or not its allocations |
| 409 | `EVENT_NOT_ON_SALE` | Right request, closed doors |
| 409 | `ALLOCATION_UNAVAILABLE` | **Someone else got there first** |

Response `expiresAt` is *recorded, not yet enforced* — nothing sweeps expired holds today.

To reproduce the race, run this request with the Collection Runner at high iteration count against a one-seat allocation and count `201`s vs `409 ALLOCATION_UNAVAILABLE`.

Same endpoint, exercising a `general_admission` allocation with `quantity > 1` and an explicit `holderId` — a stable claimant id, so the winner of a race can be named afterwards.

`quantity` caps at `HOLD_MAX_QUANTITY = 10` per line; `HOLD_MAX_LINES = 20` per request. Those are ceilings that keep one request from holding the lock over a whole stadium — not the real per-order limit, which is Ordering's business and does not exist yet.

item.name: Static assets
item.description: Uploaded hero images, served straight off disk by `express.static` — the local-first stopgap ADR-0005 allows.

request.description:
`GET /uploads/:filename`.

Outside the `api/v1` prefix: a stored `heroImageUrl` is dereferenced for as long as the row lives and should not stop resolving the day the API becomes v2.

Filenames carry a UUID and are never reused, so responses are `immutable, max-age=30d`. A miss is a plain `404` (`fallthrough: false`), not Nest's "Cannot GET".

Served with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` — these are attacker-supplied bytes on our origin.

Set `{{uploadFilename}}` to the basename from a `heroImageUrl`. In S3 mode the URL points at the bucket instead and this request does not apply.
